title: Bypassing SynthID AI detection on art assets
author: MelodramaticShape
selftext:
**I want to be clear on this post -- this is not meant to say you should not comply with AI disclosures, but this is a way to mitigate immediate confrontation/harassment for using AI in your development process.**  
  
A common tactic I've seen for discrediting an AI-generated or assisted game is to immediately throw Steam capsule or game screenshots into a SynthID detector. If you are not aware, SynthID is a human-imperceptible fingerprint encoded into images generated by participating SynthID partners (OpenAI, Google, etc.).  
  
**Any screenshots of your game where Gemini or OpenAI-generated assets are present are likely to be flagged by a SynthID detector.** 

There are a number of free sources that will strip watermarks from your images. If you have a GPU made in the past 10 years, you can use Qwen Image. If you want an easy local solution I would recommend [Synthid-Bypass](https://github.com/cebeuq/Synthid-Bypass).

This has been my TED talk, thank you.

replies.author: neurid
replies.body:
Images generated by ChatGPT or Gemini (and whoever else watermarks their gens) and used as textures are still, ultimately, images with the SynthID watermark. If those textures appear within a screenshot, regardless of the viewing angle within the screenshot (and so long as it is large close enough to the viewer within the screenshot), then that watermark will be perfectly identifiable to either SynthID detection systems.

It's just like how you can use your phone to take a picture from across the room of a computer screen that displays a watermarked image and SynthID will still be able to detect it, except instead of your phone taking a picture it's a game screenshot with a generated texture present within it.

comments.author: CrowdGoesWildWoooo
comments.body:
You do notice that there’s already a lot of wrong even from your example. 

If you have only 7 reviews, that means your wishlist and conversion game sucks, no amount help or non-AI disclosure would help dig your way out. Unless you are planning for a streamer bait friendslop, most game sales would occur pretty near the launch, if you can’t score during launch period unfortunately either your game is uninteresting, or your marketing sucks.

Another is you can’t expect buyers to make a comprehensive review (they could, but it’s not an expectation), mostly they would just tell you how it’s good or it’s bad. Maybe if you are giving away a free copy to someone as beta tester then I guess it’s fair that there’s some expectation on your side, but this is someone buying your final product. If it sucks you only have yourself to blame.

Still related to the previous point, at least in this sub I would happily give a more constructive feedback, but again as a buyer, I couldn’t care less to make a lengthy feedback, sometimes the game just sucks so bad that unfortunately the only way to summarize it is just “AI Slop”, because otherwise this game would not exist if not for AI. 

Most people know asset flip games from just a few looks, we call games like friend slop, like do you think they don’t have the same bad stigma. However, there’s a major difference, asset flip games don’t come like flood, the number of new games popping up on steam was unprecedented. As bad as it is asset flip still a great deal of effort or engineering hurdle just to get it into prod, even if everything is just asset flip. 

Mind you the whole point I am making isn’t saying asset flip is “better” because there’s a human in the loop, but being able to take a bunch of reused or free asset to turn it into a game that can even boot, is still a great deal of effort and technical challenge, that it’s basically becomes a natural barrier. 

I spent half an hour just now going through steam curator “AI slop” list, I can assure you that people review bombing is nowhere as bad as you described. You only see them on major games and when big events like Steam Next, and mainly because coverage of major media outlet. 

Some people actually made a comprehensive review like “I try not to be judgy with the dev using AI, but …”, I mean a lot of these games won’t even pass my sniff test or even from top to bottom is just AI generated stuffs, but looking at the review, it’s actually very forgiving. And no, people refunding and then making the review “AI slop, don’t buy” isn’t as common. I’d suggest you just do the same exercise instead of taking whatever in the media at face value. 

There are a lot of legitimate comment instead of quick “AI slop”, that I am surprised people actually care to write that much even if the review end up being negative. That just means your game have to be incredibly, like incredibly bad that people would shot your game down. 

\> You’re challenging the argument that I’ve never made.

You kind of do with that attitude. You work with the assumption that everyone who goes into your game have 0.1 hours of play time and decide to refund are just trolls who go there to throw bad reviews at AI generated game, while it can just be someone going into your game, play 10 minutes, and the game doesn’t pass the sniff test, which I can tell you a lot are like that, and going back to my earlier point, that this game would have never even see the light, if it were not for AI which if you kind of want to condense that into a point, it’s an “AI slop”.
